content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper reconsiders the effect of homology on GCNs. This article studies the reasons affecting the aggregation of GCNs from the perspective of neighborhood distribution. The paper finds that neighborhood structure and range are key factors for GCNs to distinguish node neighbors. Therefore, the paper designs a multi-hop neighborhood aggregation method (GCN-PND) based on the similarity of neighborhood distribution. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of GCN-PND.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:
This paper is well structured and well written. The problem to be solved is well defined. The experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
Cons:
(1) I think the article lacks innovation. Strategies in aggregating neighbors are very common approaches.
(2) Why assume that the data are Normal distributions, not other distributions?
(3) The experiment is not complete enough, and the author is suggested to supplement the experiment, such as parameter analysis, ablation experiment, etc.
(4) Some pictures are confusing. For example, in Figure 3, we don't know what the different colors mean.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: This article is well-written and clearly structured.
Quality: The article lacks some important experiments.
Novelty: The article is not innovative enough.
Reproducibility: The article has open-source code and is reproducible.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The article is well-written and not innovative enough.
In summary, the quality of this paper is far below the acceptance bar for ICLR due to its unclear innovation, and limited contribution.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper discusses how the neighborhood distribution affects the aggregation scheme in GCNs and concludes that neighborhood structure and neighborhood range are two key factors to promote the distinguishability. Based on this conclusion, the paper proposes a graph convolution network (GCN-PND), which updates graph topology based on the similarity between local neighborhood distribution of nodes and designs extensible aggregation from multi-hop neighbors. Experimental results on semi-supervised and fully-supervised node classification support the claim that the method is effective on heterophilous datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. The method for updating the adjacency matrix with connection to similar nodes appears novel and effective.

2. The experimental results on semi-supervised and fully-supervised node classification show that the method outperforms several state-of-the-art methods on heterophilous datasets.

Weaknesses:
1. More theoretical supports are expected, especially in the part discussing the impact of neighborhood distribution. Some of the conclusions are based on case studies and intuitions. For instance, the conclusion that a "good” graph structure can improve the performance of GCN is based on a case study of t-SNE visualization on the dataset Squirrels.

2. In Section 3, assumption (2) states that there are several edge distributions in class c and edges around node i, but later for the convenience of research, a unified edge distribution is defined in the same class. This makes assumption (2) problematic.

3. In Section 3, the notations are somewhat too complicated, and some symbols seem to be redundant, which makes it difficult to follow. For instance, the neighborhood structure distribution $ \mathcal{S}_i(\theta, J)$ is only mentioned in its definition, but not used in subsequent parts. Moreover, some notations are not in a unified form: some of the vectors are marked with an arrow, but others are not.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper includes necessary references and clarifies how the proposed method is different from them. There are a number of mistakes in the texts and equations. Here are the details:

1. In Paragraph 4 of the introduction, after "in the heterophily settings", a full stop is missing. In Paragraph 4 of section 3, before "Therefore, node feature", a full stop is missing.

2. Some of the “nodes” in section 3 seems to refer to node embeddings, but not the nodes themselves.

3. Several operators in equations, for instance, exp(), deg(), diag() and softmax(), are not marked with "\operatorname", but simply in math mode.

4. There are several grammatical mistakes in section 3. For example, in the paragraph of "Empirical investigation for neighborhood distribution": "with the increase of edge(s)", "homophily may not (be) the", "It is likely that the aggregated feature(s)".

5. In Equation 10: the $e_{ij}$ in the denominator should be $e_{ik}$.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper provides a discussion on how the neighbourhood distribution affects the aggregation scheme in GNNs. The methods for updating the graph structure could be effective. The method also achieves rather good results in node classification tasks. However, more theoretical justifications are expected. Moreover, the clarity of the discussion on neighbourhood distribution could be enhanced, and higher presentation quality of the paper is expected.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a new model for learning on heterophilous graphs. The main ingredients are modifying the graph topology and neighborhood aggregation from multi-hop neighbors. The experiments conducted on six standard heterophilous datasets show improvements over other models.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
My main concerns regarding the paper are the clarity of writing and limited experiments; see detailed comments below.

1. The main weakness is poor writing clarity, which significantly complicates the reading. For instance, Section 3 is extremely hard to follow. In particular, the last three sentences of the first paragraph and the whole second paragraph. Some terminology is not introduced. E.g., “neighborhood structure distribution” is not defined, and thus the definition of S_i is unclear. Then, the phrase “a single node contains incomplete class feature” is not clear. Similarly, the phrase “There are several edge distributions in class c”. To make this part understandable, it is important to formally introduce the notation used.

2. Some explanations regarding (3) would be helpful. If neighbor classes are random (with the required distribution), then I do not understand why we get the normal distribution here. Assume that a node has one neighbor, and this neighbor is of class 0 or 1 with probability 0.5. Then, we get a mixture of normal distributions instead.

3. The observations discussed in “Empirical investigation for neighborhood distribution” are quite straightforward. The fact that it is not homophily that affects the performance of GNNs has already been observed in several papers. Similar synthetic experiments with varying homophily ratio are given, e.g., in Ma et al. (2021).

4. The experiments use six standard heterophilous datasets. However, recently concerns have been raised regarding their usage. First, they are small and from limited domains (Lim et al., 2021). Also, a huge fraction of duplicates was recently found in Squirrel and Chameleon [1]. Good performance can often be caused by such duplicates, and removing them highly affects the ranking of models.

[1] A critical look at evaluation of GNNs under heterophily: Are we really making progress? 2022. https://openreview.net/pdf?id=tJbbQfw-5wv

Some minor comments:
- Table 2, column Wisconsin – the bold number is not the best one.
- Why k \in {1,2} in (4)?

There are some typos/errors:
- Some missing spaces (usually before parenthesis)
- Missing articles throughout the text
- end of page 2: “indicates nodes from different classes are more likely to connect edges”
- incorrect quotation marks are often used
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The clarity is quite poor; see the details above. Regarding novelty, to the best of my knowledge, the proposed architecture differs from the existing works.
content.summary_of_the_review: My main concern is poor clarity of writing which significantly complicates the reading and prevents thorough evaluation of the paper. (See details in "Strength And Weaknesses" above). The experimental results are also limited. Thus, I recommend rejection.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: Authors analyzed the impact of neighborhood distributions on the performance of GCN for node classification tasks and showed that homophily is not the key factor of the performance. Inspired by that analysis, authors propose the framework that updates links for a given graph so that the GCN utilizes better neighbor information. The proposed model, GCN-PND, outperforms other baseline models on various graph datasets, including heterophilous datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
* Strengths
- Authors analyze the important factor for GCN performance
- Updating the graph structure is an interesting approach to study more.
- The proposed method outperforms the baseline on various datasets

* Weaknesses
- Argument agains homophily is well verified, but the argument about distinguishability or the optimal direction authors want is not clear. It should be clearly stated with the clear support. Currently, even the definition of distinguishability is not easy to find.
- While authors claim that homophily isn't an important factor for the GCN, the graph update authors provide seems to enforce the homophily based on the embedding space. From the naive direct thinking, these seem contradictory. Authors need to clarify the presentation so that authors do not become confused. A recommended way could clarify 1) what are the clear definition of characteristics or the objective function  authors need to achieve with respect to neighbors and 2) whether the proposed update is aligned with that direction.
- Graph update seems to play a significant role. In this case, more sensitivity analysis is recommended in the ablation study. For instance, how can we choose the lambda value? Particularly for the hetrophilious datasets, what is the optimal value of lambda because the graph update seems to add the homophily.

* Details
- The overall algorithm is not very clear, How is the graph update placed in the middle of the algorithm? Is that in the part of back propagation? If so, how some threshold-based addition/deletion is handled? If not, how is the graph update incorporated with the other part of learning?
- What is the role of the edge deletion? If the direction of graph update is to cluster similar embeddings, how can it be linked to the analysis that authors have? And how is the proposed update working in a good way for heterophilious networks?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- Clarity can be improved
  - Some definition or objective such as distinguishability is missing. Clear definition would be helpful for understanding.
  - More alignment between analysis and proposed algorithms or more clarification between their relationships would be great to have.
content.summary_of_the_review: Authors propose a novel interesting approach to consider. However, even though the proposed mechanism seems to work well for the evaluation datasets, the overall presentation is not clear in the sense of  why we aim that direction of update. The analysis shown in the first half seems more opposite to the proposed method. Either the presentation needs to be clarified or some analysis needs to be enforced to make better coherence throughout the paper.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.title: Misattribution of datasets
content.comment:
The paper misattributed the authorship of the Chameleons and Squirrels datasets. These datasets were proposed in this ICLR submission:

https://openreview.net/forum?id=HJxiMAVtPH

The Pei et al. paper cited by the authors took the Squirrel and Chameleons datasets and used those for benchmarking, but had nothing to do with the creation of the datasets. The correct citation for the paper which proposed the datasets is:

```bibtex
>@article{musae,
          author = {Rozemberczki, Benedek and Allen, Carl and Sarkar, Rik},
          title = {{Multi-Scale Attributed Node Embedding}},
          journal = {Journal of Complex Networks},
          volume = {9},
          number = {2},
          year = {2021},
}
```

display_title: Thanks for pointing out the Misattribution of datasets

content.title: Thanks for pointing out the Misattribution of datasets
content.comment: We will add the correct citation of Squirrel and Chameleons datasets in our paper.
